questions.question: What does the perpendicular segment represent in the point-line distance picture?
options: A direction vector of the line itself.
The longest segment from the point to the line.
A segment that must pass through the origin.
The shortest segment from the point to the line.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular segment from the point to the line is the shortest such segment, and its length is the point-line distance.

It is the shortest segment from the point to the line, not the longest; any other segment from the point to the line is longer (hypotenuse vs leg).
It need not pass through the origin; the perpendicular segment runs from the point to the line, regardless of where the origin is.

questions.question: When is the distance from a point to a line equal to zero?

Whenever the line is horizontal.
Exactly when the point lies on the line.
Exactly when the line has zero direction vector.
questions.explanation: The distance is zero exactly when the point lies on the line.

questions.skill_detail: conceptual: Key result: distance zero iff point lies on the line.
option_explanations: The distance is zero exactly when the point lies on the line; the origin attains zero distance only for lines through $0$, e.g. the line $\ell(t)=(1+t,0,0)$ stays distance $1$ from $0$.

questions.question: In a parametrised line $\ell(t)$, what role does $t$ play in the distance calculation?
options: It ranges over all points of the line.
It fixes the outside point.
It must always be an integer.
It changes the dimension of the space.
questions.explanation: In $\ell(t)$, the parameter $t$ ranges over all real values, giving every point on the line; the distance is minimised over $t$.
questions.source_support: Coordinate method: minimise $\|\ell(t)-A\|$.
questions.review_notes: Manually designed in LA high-quality batch 14; concept-specific stem and plausible distractors.
questions.skill_detail: conceptual: Coordinate method: minimise $\|\ell(t)-A\|$.
option_explanations: It does not fix the outside point; $t$ parametrises the line $\ell(t)$, while the outside point $A$ is fixed independently of $t$.
It need not be an integer; $t$ is a real parameter ranging over all of $\mathbb R$ (or an interval), giving every point on the line.
It does not change the dimension of the space; $t$ is a scalar parameter along the line, and the ambient dimension is fixed.
